findings.title: rows.slice(1, limit + 1) drops the first row of every page
findings.explanation: The slice starts at index 1, so the newest invoice on every page is silently skipped. Page 1 loses its first invoice, and each later page loses the row right after the cursor. Those invoices never reach the client. Use rows.slice(0, limit) to keep the first `limit` rows and discard only the extra look-ahead row.

findings.title: next_before cursor is derived from the wrong slice and can be inconsistent
findings.explanation: With the off-by-one slice, page has limit rows when hasMore is true, so page[page.length - 1] is rows[limit], which is the look-ahead row. The cursor is then the id of the extra row, and since the query uses id < cursor, that row is skipped too. After fixing the slice to (0, limit), page[page.length - 1] is rows[limit - 1], which is the correct cursor. Add a test that checks the cursor equals the id of the last returned invoice.

findings.title: Edge cases: limit = 0 and invalid limit values
findings.explanation: If limit can be 0, hasMore is true whenever any row exists, but page is empty, so page[page.length - 1] is undefined and throws a TypeError (500). Also confirm that limit is validated as an integer with a sane minimum and maximum, since limit + 1 is now passed to SQL and a string value would concatenate (e.g. '10' + 1 = '101') if it is not parsed to a number. Enforce 1 <= limit <= MAX and numeric parsing before this code.

findings.title: Missing tests for pagination boundaries
findings.explanation: This change is about boundary behavior, and the bug above would have been caught by tests. Add cases for: fewer than limit rows, exactly limit rows (next_before null), limit + 1 rows (next_before set, no row skipped or duplicated across pages), an empty result, and walking all pages to confirm the full set is returned exactly once.

findings.title: Ordering relies on id only and the max page size effectively grows by one
findings.explanation: Ordering by id DESC is a stable, unique key, so cursor pagination is fine. However, if there is a maximum limit cap, the query now fetches cap + 1 rows, so be aware of that when tuning the cap or index usage. An index on (org_id, id DESC) keeps this efficient.

Review this pull request.

## Fix next_before when the last page is exactly full

When the last page had exactly `limit` invoices, `next_before` was still set, so the web app made one extra request that came back empty. This fetches `limit + 1` rows to know whether another page exists.

## Diff

```diff
diff --git a/src/routes/invoices.ts b/src/routes/invoices.ts
index b9edb19..8e99e4e 100644
--- a/src/routes/invoices.ts
+++ b/src/routes/invoices.ts
@@ -19,11 +19,13 @@ invoicesRouter.get('/', async (req, res) => {
       WHERE org_id = $1 AND ($2::bigint IS NULL OR id < $2)
       ORDER BY id DESC
       LIMIT $3`,
-    [req.user.orgId, before ?? null, limit],
+    [req.user.orgId, before ?? null, limit + 1],
   )
+  const hasMore = rows.length > limit
+  const page = rows.slice(1, limit + 1)
   res.json({
-    invoices: rows.map(serializeInvoice),
-    next_before: rows.length === limit ? rows[rows.length - 1].id : null,
+    invoices: page.map(serializeInvoice),
+    next_before: hasMore ? page[page.length - 1].id : null,
   })
 })
```
